name: semantic-grounding-check-integrations

messages.content:
Teaching examples below use fictional Example-prefixed entities. They are not additional dataset records.

You are the last verification step in a data-extraction pipeline, judging a Product -> Integrates -> Product relationship extracted from a quote copied verbatim from a real web page. Judge only what the quote itself supports -- do not use outside knowledge about whether the named entities actually exist or actually have this relationship in reality.

Judge these things:

1. is_named_organization -- not applicable to this relationship type (both endpoints are products, not organizations). Always answer true.

2. relationship_actually_happened -- true if the quote states the integration as a real, already-in-place fact, including a direct declarative claim ("X integrates with Y", "X is integrated with Y", "Two ways X is integrated with Y") even if the quote doesn't elaborate the underlying technical mechanism. False only if the tense or wording itself signals the integration is not yet real -- a plan, hope, intention, roadmap item, or pending decision ("plans to integrate", "is working on integrating", "aims to connect", "X and Y partner to integrate their platforms") -- a signed partnership or agreement announcing an intent to integrate is not by itself confirmation the integration is live -- or explicitly says it was cancelled, derailed, postponed, or never came to be.

3. relationship_claim_supported -- true if the quote names both products together with an explicit integration/connection cue (e.g. "integrates with," "syncs with," "connects to," "embedded in," "sends data to," "pulls from") describing them, even if the quote itself doesn't detail the underlying data-exchange mechanism. Reject: a commercial partnership or investment announcement with no stated technical connection, a generic compatibility claim not naming this specific product (e.g. "works with most EHRs"), or a mention of both products in the same sentence/list with no integration cue at all (e.g. a logo wall, an award list, an unrelated co-mention).

4. is_third_party_vendor — true if the object is a genuinely independent company/product, separate from the subject vendor. False if the quote frames the object as part of the subject's own product line — via possessive naming, first-person language, a compound brand containing the vendor's name, "built with [vendor]'s technology," or the quote naming a single combined product/brand that explicitly merges the vendor's name (or another of its products) with the object's name (e.g. "ExampleCare Care-ExampleModule") — as opposed to language merely describing one product being deeply embedded in or built for another (a "native X integration," "built for X," "available within X" partner product is still third-party even when tightly embedded). If a combined brand name literally containing both the vendor's name and the object's name appears anywhere in the quote, that overrides any "native/integration" phrasing elsewhere in the same sentence — treat as false regardless. Judge only from the quote/evidence context, not outside knowledge of corporate ownership — a plainly-named separate company with none of these cues is a real third party even if you recall an acquisition. The vendor's own known products/aliases: {{target_product_aliases}}. If the object matches any of these -- even under a different marketing name, with a trademark symbol, or with added/removed words -- it is NOT a third-party vendor; treat is_third_party_vendor as false.

5. is_customer_facing_integration — For an Integrates relationship only: true if the quote describes an actual product-to-product integration a customer would use. False if the object is backend infrastructure the subject vendor built its own product on top of — a cloud host, an LLM/AI provider, a database or API the vendor consumes to power its own features — even when the quote uses partnership language like "collaboration with" or "leveraging."

6. is_specific_named_entity — For an Integrates relationship only: true if the object is a specific, real, named product or company. False if it's a generic product category or system type rather than a specific product (e.g. "EHR/PMS," "practice management system," "scheduler," "EHRs") or an anonymized description with no real name given. A generic category is not a specific named integration partner even when the quote genuinely describes the subject vendor connecting to something of that type.

7.subject_is_the_claimant — this page is {{source_url}}. Answer false in one situation only: the quote is a list, or a heading above a list, where the page's owner is enumerating many things it works with, and the subject is simply one entry in that list with no sentence of its own. In that case the claim belongs to the page owner and says nothing about the subject. Answer true in every other case, including when the speaker is the object rather than the subject — "integration with our platform" written by the partner still states a real connection between the two. Who is speaking does not matter; being an unmentioned item on someone else's list does.

8. reason — one or two sentences, in plain language, saying why you answered as you did. Name the exact words in the quote that convinced you, and say who those words are about. If you answered true, state which phrase states the relationship between these two specific products. If no phrase does, say so and answer false above.

Example (false): "the staff checks the patient into ExampleBooking, where they are automatically checked into the Practice Management System" — "Practice Management System" is a category, not a named product.

Example (false — backend infrastructure): "Suki Assistant, in collaboration with Google Cloud, will leverage Google Cloud's Vertex AI platform to expand its assistive capabilities." Google Cloud is hosting/AI infrastructure Suki built its own feature on, not a customer-facing integration.

Example (true — real integration): "Suki's partnership with Azalea Health... embedding Suki's ambient listening capability into the Azalea Health EHR." This is a genuine product-to-product integration a customer uses, even though it also says "partnership."

Example (false — someone else's list): on a page at hub.example, the heading "We've perfected connectivity with:" above a list containing both ExampleBooking and ExamplePartner. "We" is ExampleHub, the page's owner. The list says ExampleHub connects to each item; it says nothing about ExampleBooking connecting to ExamplePartner.

Quote: {{quote}}
Extracted relationship: {{subject}} ({{subject_type}}) -{{relation}}-> {{object}} ({{object_type}})
Page: {{source_url}}

Evidence context:
{{evidence_context}}

Judge the quote together with this isolated source subsection, and with the page it came from. A control state, testimonial attribution, or logo-wall context may support integration only when the subsection includes an explicit integration/connection cue attributable to the subject. A heading above a list is a statement by the page's owner about that whole list — it is not a statement that any two items inside the list are connected to each other.

The evidence may also include an argument from an earlier step that read the whole page. Treat it as a claim, not as page text: it can tell you where to look and why two parts of the page connect, but it is not itself evidence. A confident argument with nothing on the page behind it is not enough.
